questionStem: A 6-year-o ld boy is brought to the physician by his parents because he continues to wet the bed approx imately five times weekly. He has never had a sustained dry period longer than 7 days. Most of the "accide nts" occur during the first 3 hours of the night and occas ionally during dreams in which he imagines himself urinating. He is afraid to go to friends' houses for sleepovers because of this problem. He worries that his friends would make fun of him if they knew, and he freque ntly feels bad about hims,elf "because I pee the bed like a baby." He was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus 1 year ago. It is well controlled with insulin, and he is compliant with the medication regimen. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's bed-wetting?

choices.E: Urinary overflow incontinence secondary to diabetes mellitus

correctExplanation: Primary enuresis refers to episodic urinary incontinence occurring in children older than 5 years. The episodes commonly lead to adjustment problems and low self-esteem. The pathogenesis of primary enuresis most common ly involves a delay in maturation, though it may alternatively be related to a small functiona l bladder capacity or genetic factors. Along with a voiding diary, patients with nocturnal enuresis should undergo a thorough history, physical examination, and urinalysis to rule out medical causes (eg, bladder dysfunction, urinary tract infection). Many patients with primary enuresis spontaneous ly improve, though motivational therapy (eg, rewarding the patient for urinating prior to bed or having incontinence-free nights) may hasten improvement. In patients with persistent enuresis or enuresis associated with emotional problems, management with enuresis alarms or desmopressin is indicated.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Generalized anxiety disorder (Choice A) is an anxiety disorder that features excessive worrying about a range of topics with associated functional impairment. This patient's worry is specific to nocturna l urinary incontinence. Oppositional defiant disorder (Choice B) manifests as a persistent pattern of angry mood, defiant behavior, and vindictiveness that causes distress and impaired functioning in the child or their caretakers. This child's enuresis is not a voluntary behavior. Social phobia (Choice D), also known as social anxiety disorder, refers to an excessive fear of scrutiny, embarrassment, or rejection in social or performance situations leading to significant distress or impaired functioning. This patient's anxiety in social situations is secondary to enuresis. - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - -- -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - ~, ~ ~ r,

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld man with Parkinson disease is brought to the physician by his wife for a follow-up examination 6 weeks after pramipexole was added to his regimen of carbidopa- levodopa to manage increasingly severe bradykinesia. The patient reports improved movement and greater stability with walking. His wife says that he has become increasingly suspicious of her and has accused her of infidelity. Last week, she awoke during the night and found him sitting in the living room with his hunting rifle on his knees. The patient had insisted that a prowler or "her paramour" was sneaking around the house, and he intended to "teach him a lesson he won't have to learn twice." The patient has no history of psychiatric illness, but his wife says he has seemed depressed and has had decreased appetite and motivation during the past 4 weeks. The patient just shrugs his shoulders in response to his wife's comment. He has hypertens ion control led with lisinopril and hyperlipidemia controlled with lovastatin. His blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg. Examination shows less rigidity and increased arm swing compared with examination results 6 weeks ago. On mental status examination, he is coopera tive and superficially polite. He has a mildly dysphoric mood and restricted affect. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's change in mental status?
correctExplanation: Pramipexole increases dopamine concentrations in several brain areas. In the dorsal striatum, an increased dopamine concentration leads to improvement in Parkinson symptoms. In the ventral striatum, dopamine-enhancing medications may lead to mood dysregulation or depression (commonly manifesting with somatic or neurovegetative symptoms). In the limbic system, an increased dopamine concentration leads to psychotic symptoms such as paranoid delusions, hallucinations, and an incongruent affect (as demonstrated by this patient). Distressing psychotic symptoms in the setting of Parkinson disease treatment are typically managed with antipsychotic medication or a decreased dose of the inciting medication.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Delusional disorder (Choice B) is characterized by the presence of one or more delusions (fixed, false beliefs) for a month or longer without other psychotic symptoms. This patient does not demonstrate one circumscribed delusion, instead presenting with general paranoia (against his wife, her "paramour," a prowler). Further, the onset of psychotic symptoms correlates with the initiation of pramipexole. questionStem: A 25-yea r-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her mother, who reports that the patient has been threatening her at home during the past 2 weeks. The patient has a 5-year history of schizophrenia. Her psychiatric symptoms had been "fairly" well controlled with oral quetiapi ne for 6 months, but she reports that she stopped taking her medication 6 weeks ago because it was sedating her. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Mental status exam ination shows an agitated mood and a guarded affect. She appears to be responding to internal stimuli. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacothe rapy?

choices.B: Switch from quetiapine to amitripty line

correctExplanation: Schizophrenia is characterized by delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, and negative symptoms (eg, alogia, apathy, flattened affect). Treatment requires long-term antipsychotic medication. In patients with a partial response to an antipsychotic, a dose increase should be considered. However, intolerable side effects may limit the maximum acceptable dose. Quetiapine is an atypica l antipsychotic medication that primarily antagonizes dopamine-2 receptors and serotonin receptors. Quetiapine also antagonizes histamine receptors, adrenoreceptors, and muscarinic receptors, leading to sedation, weight gain, orthostatic hypotension, and anticholinergic side effects (eg, dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation). This patient experiencing the combination of intolerable sedation (leading to nonadherence) and incomplete control of psychotic symptoms should be trialed on a less sedating antipsychotic medication. Aripiprazo le is an antipsychotic medication with a lower affinity for histamine and acetylcho line receptors and is therefore less likely to cause sedation.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Increasing the dosage of quetiapine (Choice A) would likely worsen this patient's sedation. She has already self-discontinued quetiapine because of sedation, so increasing the dosage would make her even less likely to adhere to the medication regimen. Switching from quetiapine to amitriptyline (Choice B) or bupropion (Choice D), antidepressant medications, would not address this patient's psychotic symptoms. This patient should be switched to a different antipsychotic medication. Switching from quetiapine to chlorpromazine (Choice E) would be less likely to resolve the patient's sedation. Chlorpromazine is a low­ potency typical antipsychotic that antagonizes histamine receptors, adrenoreceptors, and muscarinic receptors. It commonly causes sedation. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: An 86-year-o ld woman is brought to the physician because of confusion , forgetfu lness , and lethargy for 6 weeks. She lives by herse lf and has been functio ning inde pendently . She has hypertens ion, hypercho lestero lemia, and osteoarthritis of the lumbar spine and hips. Her drug regimen includes hydrochlorothiazide, captopri l, naproxen , gemfibrozi l, and lovastat in. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 87/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Reflexes bilaterally are brisk, and muscle strength in the upper and lower extremities is exce llent. On menta l status examination , she is oriented to person but not to time and place and is unable to remember three objects after 2 minutes; she cannot perform serial sevens and is frustrated when she cannot answer proverb or judgment questions . A CT scan of the head shows mild d iffuse cerebra l atrophy with no lesions. An x-ray of the chest shows normal findings. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the change in mental status?

choices.B: Adverse effect of hydrochlorothiazide therap Yi
choices.C: Adverse effect of lovastat in therapy

correctExplanation: Electro lyte derangements such as hyponatremia or hypernatremia can cause altered menta l status. Hyponatremia can be acute or chronic. Acute hyponatremia occurs in 24 to 48 hours and commonly presents with symptoms of nausea, malaise, lethargy, obtundation or coma, and seizures secondary to cerebra l edema, as water is drawn into the neurona l cells in the setting of hypotonic interstitia l fluid. Given the rapid decline in sodium, symptoms can even present with sodium concentrations of 130 mEq/L. In chronic hyponatremia, however, symptoms generally do not present until the hyponatremia has become significant (usually less than 120 mEq/L). Symptoms include fatigue, nausea, forgetfu lness, lethargy, and confusion. questionStem: A 35-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, has had episodes of anxiety, bloating, fatigue, irritability, and breast tenderness for the past 2 years. Her symptoms begin about 10 days before menses and cease with the onset of menses. Physical examina tion is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in patient care?

choices.A: Reassura nce and reexam ination in 6 months
choices.B: Instruction to keep a diary of symptoms for the next two menstrual cycles
choices.D: Measureme nt of serum thyrox ine (T 4), thyroid-stimulating hormone , and prolactin concentratio ns

correctExplanation: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) consists of affective and somatic symptoms occurring in the week before menses. According to the DSM-5, patients must demonstrate at least five symptoms. The symptoms must include at least one mood symptom (affective !ability, marked irritability, depressed mood, or anxiety) and at least one of the following symptoms: anhedonia, concentration difficulties, decreased energy, hypersomnia or insomnia, increased or decreased appetite, a sense of being overwhelmed, and physical symptoms (eg, breast tenderness, muscle or joint pain, sensation of bloating, weight gain). The symptoms must begin to improve within a few days after menses onset and resolve during the week after menses. The diagnosis is established by the patient's prospective documentation of symptoms in relation to at least two menstrual cycles. The pathogenesis is likely related to modulation of neurotransmitters such as serotonin secondary to changes in estrogen and progesterone concentrations. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are indicated in patients with moderate to severe PMDD, whereas patients with mild PMDD may benefit from counseling about stress reduction and lifestyle changes.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Reassurance and reexamination in 6 months (Choice A) would be inappropriate in this patient who is likely to have a PMDD diagnosis and may benefit from active management with medications or stress reduction techniques. Behavior modification therapy (Choice C) emphasizes reinforcement and punishment of certain behaviors. It is commonly utilized in autism spectrum disorder and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. However, this patient is not demonstrating problematic behaviors that require modification. Measurement of serum thyroxine (T 4), thyroid-stimulating hormone, and prolactin concentrations (Choice D) are unnecessary in patients who meet diagnostic criteria for PMDD. Mood changes related to thyroid dysfunction are accompanied by other physical examination signs of thyroid disease (eg, skin and hair changes) and are not typically episodic. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 48-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter 2 hours after she fell at home. Physical exam ination shows ecchymoses over the left hip and left shoulder but is otherwise normal. During evaluation, the daughter pulls the physician aside and explains that her mother has drunk excessively over the past 12 years. She freque ntly consumes several bottles of wine alone at home each day. She also reports that her mother has been forgetting to take cooking pots off the stove. When the physician continues with the evaluation, the patient behaves as if she has never met the physician before now. On cognitive examination, she recalls zero out of three objects after 5 minutes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's cognitive decline?
correctExplanation: Patients who chronically abuse alcohol typically demonstrate a significant thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency caused by poor nutritional intake, thiamine malabsorption, and impaired cellular utilization of thiamine. Over time, thiamine deficiency can result in damage and atrophy of the mammillary bodies, visible on MRI of the brain, which manifests as Wernicke encephalopathy. The typical clinical presentation of Wernicke encephalopathy is a triad of acute altered mental status, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, and ataxia. The symptoms of Wernicke encephalopathy are reversible but incre,ase the risk for developing Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (also known as Korsakoff psychosis) in chronic alcohol users if not immediately treated with high-dose thiamine. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is an irreversible condition that features anterograde and retrograde amnesia along with the consequent tendency to confabulate, or verbalize false stories or memories, to compensate for the inability to remember. This patient demonstrates an inability to form new memories after the amnesia-causing event (anterograde amnesia).
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (Choice A) is a human prion disease that presents with rapidly progressing dementia, neuropsychiatric symptoms, cerebellar dysfunction, corticospinal tract dysfunction, basal ganglia dysfunction, and stimulus-induced myoclonus. This patient does not demonstrate stimulus-induced myoclonus or cerebellar, corticospina l, or basal ganglia dysfunction. Dementia, Alzheimer type (Choice B), is the most prevalent dementia, presenting with progressive cognitive decline that begins with short-term memory impairment, progresses to apraxia and language abnormalities, and culminates in behavioral and personality changes preventing the patient from performing basic activities of daily living. Anterograde memory impairment is common, but this patient's young age is inconsistent with dementia, Alzheimer type. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her father as a new patient for a well-child examination. On entering the physician's office, the patient immediately climbs onto the physician's lap and begins talking with the physician. Her father says that his daughter has shown poor learning ability and has outbursts in school. He also says she is highly sensitive to sound. Examination shows a small, upturned nose, small chin, and long philtrum. Muscle tone is decreased. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Williams syndrome results from a sporadic or inherited deletion of contiguous genes on chromosome 7q11.23, including the elastin gene. Patients typically present with an overly friendly demeanor, emotiona l dysregulation, intellectual delay, elfin facies (strabismus, flat nasal bridge, short nose, long philtrum, wide mouth), short stature, vascular and cardiac valve abnormalities seconda ry to elastin dysfunction, structura l abnormalities of the urinary tract, and endocrine abnormalities (eg, hypothyroidism). Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing confirming a deletion on chromosome 7q 11.23. !Management involves surgica l correction of vascula r, cardiac, or other functionally significant structu ral abnormalities and antihypertensive medication if such develops.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cornelia de Lange syndrome (Choice A) results from the sporadic deletion of cohesin complex genes, which normally direct prenatal development. It is characterized by growth delay, intellectual disability, facial dysmorphia (microcephaly, arched eyebrows, small upturned nose, widely spaced teeth), and malformations of the extremities. Down syndrome (Choice B) results from trisomy of chromosome 21 and presents with characteristic physical features including broad, flat, facial features with prominent epicanthal folds and a single palmar crease. Patients with Down syndrome also present with cognitive impairment, cardiac abnormalities (eg, atrial septal defect), gastrointestinal abnormalities (eg, duodenal atresia, imperforate anus), ophthalmologic abnormalities (eg, refractive errors), and hearing loss. Prader-Wi lli syndrome (Choice C) results from the absence of paternal expression of genes on chromosome 15. Children typically present with hyperphagia (and potential obesity), short stature, impaired cognition, motor delays, and hypogonadism. questionStem: A 77-year-o ld woman comes to the physician at the request of an attorney prior to writing an advance directive. She says that she wants to have an advance directive in order to avoid putting an unnecessa ry burden on her children. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She immigrated to the USA from Poland 20 years ago. She has only an elementary school education. She was employed in a cleaning service for a hotel but stopped working 5 years ago. She lives alone and is able to perform activities of daily living independently. She participates in social activities at her church. All of her close friends are also from Poland. Physical examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. On mental status exam ination, she is nervous . She is alert and is oriented to person. She knows she is in the physician's office but does not recall the street name correctly. She knows the month and day of the week but is not sure of the exact date. She knows her address. She can recall two of three words after 5 minutes. She can subtract 7 from 100 using her fingers but is unable to subtract 7 from 93. She is unable to spell the word "world" backwards. She can draw the hands on a clock to show 10 minutes to 2 o'clock and can slowly copy a drawing of two intersecting pentagons. She demonstrates that she understands the meaning of a standardized story. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step with respect to this patient's advance directive?

choices.A: Discussion of her preferences for care
choices.C: Repeat her mental status examinat ion with an interpreter

correctExplanation: Though some cognitively impaired patients may lack capacity to make decisions about their care, cognitive ly impaired patients should not be assumed to lack decisional capacity. Though this patient illustrates mild abnormalities on brief cognitive testing (which may indicate normal aging changes in a patient with a limited education), these findings do not necessarily preclude her from making end-of­ life decisions. To meet the criteria for decisional capacity, patients must express a consisten t choice, demonstrate an understanding of the risks and benefits of the choice, demonstrate an appreciation of the significance of the choice for their personal circumstances, and illustrate an ability to reason through the options. Therefore, to assess this patient's decisional capacity and potentially write her advance directive (if the physician believes the patient possesses decisional capacity), the physician should discuss the patient's preferences for care and assess the four decisional capacity criteria specific to these decisions.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. A second examination in one week (Choice B) would be unnecessary in this patient. A fluctuating cognitive course (eg, delirium) is unlikely in this patient with mild cognitive impairment who is consistently alert, attentive (difficulty with serial ?sand spelling "world" is likely secondary to this patient's limited education given her ability to attend to and understand a story), and able to verbalize a desire to write an advance directive. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: Six hours after undergoing an appendectomy, a 4 ?-year-old man repor ts a moderately severe, diffuse headac he. He has no other symptoms. He has not ingested food or drink for 2 days . His pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Neurologic examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Headaches can be differentiated into primary and secondary headaches (eg, substances, infection, neoplasm, trauma). Headache features that raise concern for serious secondary causes include fever, focal neurologic deficits, abrupt onset, history of malignancy or trauma , and positional exacerbation. Caffeine withdrawal typically presents with headache, fatigue, depressed or irritable mood, difficu lty concentrating, gastrointestinal distress, tachycardia, hand tremor, or flu-like symptoms. The headache is common ly diffuse and pulsating, varies from mild to severe in intensity, begins within 24 hours of last caffeine consump tion , and improves once withdrawal resolves. Acute management may include over-the-counter analgesics or the administration of caffeine. Patients desiring to abstain from caffeine should gradually taper their use to prevent severe withdrawal symptoms.
incorrectExplanation: nd K. Bacteria l meningitis (Choice A) typically presents with fever and signs of meningeal irritation (nausea, irritability, confusion, anorexia, photophobia, headache, and nuchal rigidity). This patient does not demonstrate a fever or signs of meningea l irritation other than headache. Brain abscess (Choice B) typically presents with fever, focal neurologic deficits, headache, and altered mental status. This patient does not demonstrate a fever, focal neurologic deficits, or altered mental status. Cluster headaches (Choice D) are primary headaches that typica lly present with short-lived , unilatera l, severe pain in the orbital, supraorbital , or tempora l region of the head and are accompanied by ipsilateral autonomic symptoms (eg, miosis, ptosis, lacrimation, nasal congestion). This patient endorses a diffuse headache and does not demonstrate autonomic symptoms. questionStem: A 37-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because her husband is concerned that she has been having difficulty remembe ring things around the house. During the past 6 weeks, she has been forgetting to do her usual household chores. She does not think that she has a problem. She says that she does her best but often feels fatigued, especial ly when moving around a lot. She has had numbness of both legs and intermittent blurred vision during the past year. Physical examination shows pallor of the optic discs. Deep tendon reflexes at the knees and ankles are brisk bilatera lly. On mental status examination, she has an upbeat mood and affect. She is oriented to person, place, and time. She has difficulty remem bering the names of recent U.S. Presidents. There is no evidence of auditory or visual hallucinations. A T2-weighted MRI of the brain shows numerous small plaques in the periventricular white matter. A lumbar puncture is done. Which of the following findings is most likely on cerebrospina l fluid analysis?
correctExplanation: Multiple sclerosis, the most prevalent immune-mediated demyelinating disease, can present initially with lesions in several central nervous system (CNS) locations. According to the McDonald criteria for multiple sclerosis diagnosis, patients must have evidence of demyelinating lesions that are separated in time and location. This evidence can be based on subjective symptoms or imaging evidence. This patient demonstrated several episodes of optic neuritis separated in time, along with dysfunction of the dorsal column­ medial lemniscus tracts (decreased sensation), corticospinal tracts (hyperreflexia), frontal lobes (incongruent ly bright affect), and medial temporal lobe (decreased recall memory), representing separation in space. Fatigue and symptom exacerbation with exercise are common in multiple sclerosis. MRI of the brain typically shows focal white matter hyperintensities in the periventricular region, cortex, subcortical region, cerebellum, or spine. Oligoclonal bands of immunoglobulins, indicating immune overactivation, can be found in the cerebrospinal fluid but are not necessary for diagnosis. Treatment includes corticosteroids for symptomatic management of acute flares and long-term disease-modifying treatments such as interferon or monoclonal antibodies, which decrease the frequency of future episodes.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Decreased glucose (Choice A) is demonstrated in bacterial and fungal meningitis or encephalitis. Eosinophilocytosis (Choice C) is consisten t with eosinophilic meningitis secondary to parasitic infections. This patient's focal neurologic deficits and chronic course along with the absence of headache, encephalopathy (eg, decreased alertness, disorientation), or systemic signs of infection are more consisten t with multiple sclerosis. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 57-year-o ld lawyer is brought to the emergency department by police after he interrupted a church service by loudly proclaim ing that he is the Messiah. Police say that he became angry and physically confronta tional when he was asked to leave and continued to insist that he was the Messiah when police intervened . On arrival in the emergency department, he is expansive and talks loudly. He appears well groomed. On questioning, he says he has never been sick and takes no medications. He does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. He refuses to allow a physical examination and becomes irritable with the nurses. He dema nds to see the person in charge of the hospital, noting he has figured out a way to save the hospital millions of dollars. On mental status examination, he talks rapidly and abruptly shifts from topic to topic. He reports hearing the voice of God telling him that He is pleased with him. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Bipolar disorder is a mood disorder that features acute episode,s of mania. This patient's career as a lawyer indicates he is high functioning at baseline, signifying that his current behavior is an episodic change from baseline. Acute mania typically manifests with an expansive or euphoric or irritable mood, increased energy, a decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, rapid speech and thinking (as evidenced by this patient's pressured speech with a flight of ideas), irresponsibility (as evidenced by this patient's disruption of a church service), and grandiose thinking (as evidenced by this patient's confidence that his plan can save the hospital millions of dollars). Some patients demonstrate associated psychotic symptoms (eg, hallucinations, delusions). This patient's belief that he is the Messiah constitutes a grandiose de lusion. Type 1 bipolar disorder is this patient's most likely diagnosis. Though patients with type 1 bipolar disorder need to demonstrate a history of mania to meet diagnostic criteria, patients with type 2 bipolar disorder must demonstrate major depressive episodes in addition to hypomanic episodes (less severe and shorter episodes of mania without psychotic features). Management requires mood stabilizing therapy (eg, mood stabilizers or mood-stabi lizing antipsychotics) for acute mania. Once acute mood episodes resolve, patients with bipolar disorder should continue mood stabilizer maintenance therapy to prevent future episodes of mania or depression.

questionStem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. His mother states that he has had increasingly impulsive behavior and aggressive outbursts during the past year. His kindergarten and first grade teachers expressed concern about his ability to follow directions and socialize with peers. At the age of 3 years, he received treatme nt for lead exposure. Language development is appropriate; toilet training milestones have been met. His mother states that he is a picky eater. He has no history of serious illness. His mother believes that he is angry about his parents getting a divorce. He is alert and fidgety. He is at the 5th percentile for height and weight. His pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 97/60 mm Hg. Examination shows no dysmorphic features . The thyroid gland is not enlarged. Pulmonary and abdomina l examinations show no abnormalities. The upper and lower extremities are thin. Muscle tone is normal. Deep tendon reflexes are brisk. He is easily distractible, impulsive in observed play, and oppositional when his mother attempts to redirect him. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) presents with chronic symptoms of hyperactivity/impulsivity or inattention that occur in more than one setting and impair academic, social, or emotional function. Children with predominant hyperactivity symptoms are unable to sit still and may have difficulty taking turns (postulated to result from a dysregulated dopamine reward pathway), whereas children with predominant inattentive symptoms tend to daydream, process information slowly, and demonstrate difficulty in completing tasks (related to norepinephrine dysregulation). ADHD is associated with soft neurologic abnorma lities such as brief reflexes. For diagnosis, physicians must establish that the patient is functional ly impaired in severa l settings, so parents and teachers must fill out behavioral rating scales. Stimulants, which include amphetamine salts and methylphenidate, are first-line agents for treatment that increase synaptic dopamine and norepinephrine.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Projective testing by the school psychologist (Choice B) would involve the patient interpreting ambiguous stimuli (eg, Rorschach testing) as a persona lity test. This patient does not demonstrate a pathologic persona lity and this testing is inappropriate at this time. Thyroid function tests (Choice C) would assist in diagnosing thyroid dysfunction, which may present with hyperactivity. However, this patient does not demonstrate tachycardia or physical examination signs of thyroid dysfunction (eg ,skin, hair, or eye changes). \ j • - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- i. - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - -- - - - - - - - -- - r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 20-year-o ld woman comes to the physician with her husba nd because of increasing fatigue and social withdrawal. The patient reports that she has always worried about her appearance and how other people perceive her. She has difficulty shopping and states, "Every time I go into a grocery store, I feel like I might not get out alive." During the past 3 months, she has induced vomiting 6 to 10 times weekly when she feels "panicky" after eating "bad foods ." Her husband reports that she becomes anxious and irritable when she has not exercised. She has not had a menstrua l period for 6 months. Her husband expresses frustration with her problems and says that her obsessive worrying and poor self-image are ruining their marriage. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She is thin and meticu lously groomed. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 48 kg (105 lb); BMI is 18 kg/m2. Her tem perature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 50/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 102/68 mm Hg. Physical examination, including pelvic examination, shows no abnormalities. The patient states that her recent weight loss of 6.8 kg (15 lb) has made her feel less anxious and that she plans to lose more weight. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Anorexia nervosa is characterized by an intense fear of gaining weight, decreased self-worth related to body weight, and consequent restricting (eg, fasting, exercising) or binge eating/purging behavior (eg, vomiting, laxative or diuretic misuse) leading to insufficient nutrition. Patients with anorexia nervosa often have a BMI less than 17 kg/m 2, though patients with mild anorexia may demonstrate a BMI greater than 17 kg/m 2(normal BMI is 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m 2). Amenorrhea is common and reflects insufficient nutrition. Alternatively, patients with bulimia nervosa do not typically demonstrate severe malnutrition that leads to amenorrhea or a low BMI. Physical examination of patients with anorexia nervosa can show dry, scaly skin and fine hair or hair loss caused by decreased protein stores. Patients who vomit to purge can demonstrate parotid gland enlargement from salivary gland overstimulation, dental caries from gastric hydrochloric acid erosion of enamel, and scars on the knuckles secondary to abrasions from the incisors when inducing vomiting. The loss of gastric hydrochloric acid leads to hypoch lorem ia and metabolic alkalosis. In severe cases, signs of hypovolemia such as tachycardia and hypotension may be present. Treatment of anorexia nervosa is through a combined medical and psychiatric approach and involves correcting fluid and electrolyte derangements along with behavioral and pharmacologic therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. questionStem: A 4-year-o ld girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of frequent temper tantrums and extreme irritability over the past 6 months. She was born at 35 weeks' gestation and had jaundice at birth. Her 17-year-old mother reports that her daughter refuses to listen to her and will not eat foods she previously ate. The mother appears sad and states that she is overwhe lmed. The patient is at the 15th percenti le for height and weight. Physical examination shows no abnorma lities. She is very active during the examinat ion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

correctExplanation: Normal 4-year-old children play with other children , play make-believe , tell stories , understand time and counting , stand and hop on one foot, and cut their own food with supervision. Typical preschoo l-age children also demonstrate defiant behavior and are picky eaters. When children demonstrate difficult behaviors, parents should utilize ignoring and other parenting skills. Teenage parents commonly possess inadequate parenting skills and may increase their attention to the child during tantrums, reinforcing the tantrum behavior. Young parents typically benefit from parenting classes.

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 57-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of memory loss for 3 months. Examination shows a very sluggish patient with a flat affect who talks slowly and in a whisper. Initially, she replies to all mental status tests, "I don't know" or "I can't remem ber." As the physician shows a warm and supportive manner, her responses improve, so that eventual ly she recalls the main event in the news the previous evening and is able to recall two out of three objects after 5 minutes. She is told the third object. When retested just before leaving 10 minutes later, she recalls all three. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?

choices.F: Major depressive disorder with atypica l features

correctExplanation: Symptoms of major depressive disorder (MOD) include 2 or more weeks of at least five of the following symptoms: depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt or worthlessness, difficulty concentrating, psychomotor retardation, suicidal thoughts, or neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). These symptoms disrupt everyday functioning. In patients with MOD with atypical features, neurovegetative symptoms typically manifest as hypersomnia and hyperphagia. Patients with MOD with atypical features may also demonstrate situational improvements in mood, oversensitivity to interpersonal rejection, or leaden paralysis (a heavy sensation in the extremities leading to extreme psychomotor retardation). The underlying pathogenesis is believed to arise from personality and temperament characteristics that promote emotional and behavioral dysregulation in response to stressful situations such as interpersonal rejection. This patient's subjective memory loss and severe psychomotor retardation that improve as she develops a rapport with the physician likely represents a functional neurologic disorder (reflecting the conversion of emotional distress into neurologic symptoms), which is frequently comorbid with depression. When the patient's fear of interpersonal rejection by the physician decreases, her distress and consequent psychological need to convert her distress into a neurologic symptom dissipates. Treatment of atypical depressive disorder involves antidepressant medication and psychotherapy.

Patients typically present with positional headaches, nausea, vomiting, and vision changes (signs of increased intracranial pressure). Memory loss in the absence of other hydrocephalus symptoms that improves over the course of minutes is atypical. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 21-year-o ld college student is brought to the emergency department by her roommates because of a 4-day history of progressive general ized weakness and muscle cramps. She has been unable to eat solids for 2 days. Her last bowel movement was 4 days ago. Her roommates report that, during the past year, they have heard her vomiting in the bathroom after meals. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. The patient is oriented to person, place, and time and says that she feels tired. Her temperature is 36°C (96.8°F), pulse is 70/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft, and bowel sounds are decreased. Muscle strength is decreased throughout. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Bulimia nervosa (binging/purging type) involves cycles of uncontrollable eating and compensatory behaviors such as vomiting, laxative, or diuretic overuse that occur at least once a week for 3 months or more. Unlike patients with anorexia nervosa, patients with bulimia nervosa typically have a normal BMI and do not demonstrate amenorrhea. Patients with the binging/purging type of anorexia or bulimia nervosa can demonstrate dental caries from gastric hydrochloric acid erosion of enamel, parotid gland swelling from salivary gland overstimulation, and scars on the knuckles secondary to abrasions from the incisors when inducing vomiting. The loss of gastric hydrochloric acid leads to hypochloremia and metabolic alkalosis. Hypokalemia is common, as increased bicarbonate leads to renal proton-potassium exchange and consequent potassium secretion. In severe cases of bulimia nervosa, signs of hypovolemia such as tachycardia and hypotension may be present. Hypovolemia leads to increased aldosterone concentrations, resulting in further potassium secretion. As potassium is involved in the membrane potential of muscle cells (including skeletal, smooth, and cardiac muscles), hypokalemia typically leads to general weakness, muscle cramps, fatigue, palpitations, or decreased gastrointestinal motility. Treatment of bulimia nervosa is through a combined medical and psychiatric approach, and it involves correcting fluid and electrolyte derangements alongside behavioral and pharmacologic therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Arterial blood gas analysis (Choice A) may assist in diagnosing respiratory failure and acid-base derangement, though it would be less helpful than electrolyte analysis in diagnosing the cause of this patient's generalized weakness, fatigue, muscle cramping, and -- - - - - - - - - -- -r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A previously well-functioning 14-year-o ld boy is apprehended for steali ng a compact disc from a store. A court-ordered evaluat ion shows the stealing to be the latest in a series of self-defeating behaviors over the past 2 months that include incomplete homewor k assignments and truancy. He states that he has difficulty concentrating and awake ns frequentlly at night. During an interview with his family, the teenage r seems oblivious to the obvious marital discord between his parents. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Adjustment disorder refers to the onset of an emotional disturbance within 3 months of an identifiable stressor. The emotiona l disturbance manifests as marked distress out of proportion to the stressor and a significant impairment in daily school, work, or social functioning. Patients may internalize or externalize their distress, resulting in depression or anxiety symptoms or conduct disturbances (acting out), respectively. Patients with adjustment disorder do not meet criteria of anxiety, depressive, or conduct disorders. This patient has some anxiety/depression symptoms (eg, difficulty concentrating and sleeping) and conduct disturbances (eg, truancy) with a clear stressor and without meeting the criteria for anxiety, depressive, or conduct disorders. As adjustment disorder is typical ly self­ limited, the treatment of adjustment disorder commonly includes brief supportive psychotherapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Antisocial persona lity disorder (Choice B) is a cluster B personality disorder that arises from a deficit in empathy, resulting in pervasive violations of others' rights, aggression, and a hostile and manipulative attitude toward others. Personality disorders are only diagnosed in patients older than 18 years, and this patient does not yet demonstrate a persistent pattern of transgressive behavior. Conduct disorder (Choice C) refers to a persistent pattern of violating others' rights, including aggression, deceitfu l behaviors, and property destruction. Patients must demonstrate this behavior for 12 months, whereas this patient has been acting out for the past 2 months. Dysthymic disorder (Choice D), more common ly called persistent depressive disorder, refers to at least three depression symptoms (including depressed mood during more days than not) that have endured at least 2 years. This patient demonstrates two depression symptoms (impaired concentration, insomnia) for 2 months only. . - - - -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - -- - - - - - - - - - - -- - -- - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of difficulty falling asleep for 3 years. She reports that it has been even more difficult to fall asleep during the past month. Five weeks ago, her cat of 4 years was hit by a car and died. She has a generally poor appetite but has not had any recent changes in weight or appetite. She has worked as a registered nurse on the overnight shift at a skilled nursing care facility for 5 years. She says that she has never missed a day of work in 3 years, althoug h she rarely feels like getting out of bed. She states that she prefers night work because it involves less contact with families. She does not enjoy her job even though she is respected for her work and regularly receives good evaluations. She is neatly dressed. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 10/min, and blood pressure is 120/65 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormal ities. On mental status examination, she is pleasant and polite. She says she felt sad when her cat died but states that she cannot recall a time when her life did not seem sad to her. When asked about her social life, she says she has never been in a romantic relationship and states that "no one would really want me." Results of laboratory studies are within the reference range. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Reassura nce that this is normal bereaveme nt
choices.F: Supplementat ion with a multivitamin and iron

correctExplanation: Persistent depressive disorder, previously called dysthymia, refers to at least three depression symptoms that have endured for at least 2 years. By definition, patients must endorse a depressed mood on more days than not. Other symptoms of persistent depressive disorder include neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbances, appetite disturbances), impaired concentration, low self-esteem, and hopelessness. This patient also demonstrates anhedonia as evidenced by a lack of enjoyment of her job or socializing; however, she does not have at least five symptoms of major depressive disorder, making persistent depressive disorder the most accurate diagnosis. Emerging evidence indicates that persistent depressive disorder should be managed similarly to major depressive disorder: antidepressant medication plus psychotherapy is most effective. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are generally the first-line medications given their low side-effect burden. However, bupropion is also a reasonable option, and its activating effects may be useful in this patient with difficulty getting out of bed.

questionStem: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents for a physical examination prior to participating in school sports. Her parents are concerned about her academ ic performance because she has received mostly B's and C's. Her parents and older brother attended Ivy League colleges. Every time they try to discuss applying to colleges, she becomes angry and tearful and goes to her room, slamming the door and refusing to talk about it. They try to talk to her through the closed door, but she will not cooperate. They have arranged alumn i interviews for her at their own alma maters, and they are concerned that this negative attitude will impact her interviews. When they contacted her guidance counselor about their concerns and observations, he was surprised and reported that she has been diligently working on her applications with his help. She is at the 50th percentile for height and 30th percent ile for weight. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examinat ion, she is cooperative but reticent. Her speech is articulate and coherent. Wh ich of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings? ~-
correctExplanation: Parental expectations exert a strong influence on children's wel l-being. Unrealistically high expectations common ly lead to the child feeling disappointed and inadequate. These feelings may be internalized (eg, lead to depression) or externalized (eg, acting out, such as slamming the door). This patient's emotional dysregulation and uncooperative behavior when her parents communicate or imply high expectations about her academic performance is an age-appropriate reaction. Parents should critical ly examine whether their expectations are realistic and communicate acceptance to their child to avoid these emotiona l difficulties.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adjustment disorder with anxious mood (Choice A) or depressed mood (Choice B) refers to the onset of disproportionate distress manifested as anxiety or depression symptoms, respectively, within 3 months of an identifiable stressor. This patient does not demonstrate anxiety or depression symptoms. As well, her uncooperative behaviors are specific to situations when her parents communicate their high expectations, whereas patients with adjustment disorder demonstrate consistent depression, anxiety, or conduct disturbances. Dysthymic disorder (Choice C), more common ly known as persistent depressive disorder, refers to depression symptoms lasting longer than 2 years. This patient does not endorse depressive symptoms and has not illustrated behavior changes for more than 2 years. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld man who is a resident of a skilled nursing care facility is brought to the emergency department because of sweating and increas ing confusion for 2 days. He underwent a below-the-k nee amputat ion 4 weeks ago for osteomyelitis. He has a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with glybur ide. He also is receiving acetaminophen and codeine for pain, allopurino l for gout, and haloperido l for nighttime agitation. His temperature is 39.5°C (103.1 °F), pulse is 120/min, and blood pressure is 130/90 mm Hg. Muscle tone is increased. The patient is too disoriented to respond appropriate ly to questions. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit Leukocyte count Serum Na+ Glucose 50% 8000/mm 3 with a normal differentia l 154 mEq/L 175 mg/dL Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
correctExplanation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is the most likely diagnosis in this patient who has received high-potency antipsychotic medication (haloperidol). NMS is a life-threatening condition associated with the antagonism of dopamine that presents with altered mental status, muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic dysfunction (eg, tachycardia, sweating). Common causative agents are antipsychotics (especia lly high-potency antipsychotics) and antidopaminergic nausea medications. Rigidity results from dopamine antagonism in the nigrostriatal pathway, while autonomic dysfunction and hyperthermia may result from dopamine antagonism in the hypothalamus. Characteristic laboratory abnorma lities include leukocytosis and increased serum creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, and alkaline phosphatase concentrations (caused by prolonged muscle rigidity and consequent myocyte damage). Electrolyte abnormalities (eg, hypo- or hypernatremia, hypocalcemia) may also be demonstrated. Treatment is supportive and includes discontinuation of the offending medication, hydration, cooling blankets, and benzodiazepines, if needed, for agitation.

questionStem: A 47-year-o ld woman comes to the physician to request a sedative to help calm her nerves. She has had extreme anxiety and difficulty eating and sleeping since she received the diagnosis of breast cancer 10 days ago. She is married and has two children, and she worries constantly about what will happen to them if she dies. She regularly volunteers at the school library, but she has been unable to go because of her anxiety since her diagnosis. She has not felt depressed, guilty, or suicidal. She has no other history of serious medical or psychiatric illness. There is no family history of psychiatric illness. Physical examination shows a healing incision over the breast biopsy site. On mental status examination, she is anxious but shows a full range of affect. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

The emotional disturbance manifests as marked distress out of proportion to the stresso r and a significant impairment in daily school, work, or social functioning. Patients may internalize or externalize their distress, resulting in depression and anxiety symptoms or conduct disturbances, respectively. questionStem: A 25-year-o ld woman is brought to the physician by her family 1 week after the sudden onset of bizarre behavior that began after she had a disagreement with her supervisor at work. The supervisor told her fam ily that she became confused and began to accuse him of monitoring her phone calls and watching her every move because he wanted to fire her. Her work performance had been fine. She told her husband that she heard the voices of her coworkers talking about her when she was driving home from work 2 days ago. She used cocaine briefly 5 years ago. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, she is oriented to person and place but not to date. She is unsure why she is being evaluated, and her answers to questions are incomprehensib le at times. She admits to being worried and depressed about her coworkers being "after her." Laboratory studies are within normal limits, and toxicology screening shows traces of marijuana. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

correctExplanation: This patient meets the diagnostic criteria for brief psychotic disorder. Brief psychotic disorder is characterized by the acute onset of one or more psychotic symptoms (eg, delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior) lasting less than 1 month. This patient is experiencing a paranoid delusion, disorganized speech, and auditory hallucinations. Risk factors for brief psychotic disorder include stressful life events and personality disorders. Treatment may include hospitalization and antipsychotic treatment depending on symptom severity and functional impairment, though some symptoms or the entire presentation may resolve without medications.

Adjustment disorder (Choice A) refers to the onset of disproportionate distress within 3 months of an identifiable stressor and may be associated with anxiety, depression, or conduct disturbances. The onset of this patient's psychotic symptoms years after cocaine use is inconsistent with cocaine-induced psychotic disorder. Post-traumatic stress disorder (Choice D) refers to symptoms of intrusive thoughts and memories of trauma, hyperarousal, avoidance of trauma reminders, or negative mood/thoughts resulting from a traumati c event (such as a life-threatening motor vehicle collision) and lasting more than one month. This patient did not experience a life-threatening incident, intrusive memories, avoidance of trauma - -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - - r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents because of behavior problems since starting preschool 3 months ago. Her parents report that she was adopted at 2 weeks of age and little is known about her biologic parents. Her teachers report that she is more active than her peers, is easily frustrated, and has frequent tantrums. She is not yet toilet trained. She is at the 20th percentile for height and weight. Physical examination shows a thin upper lip, a narrow philtrum, and bilateral palmar creases. Her gait is normal. On mental status examination, she speaks clearly, communicating in two- to three-word phrases. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Alcohol is a proven teratogen, since alcohol use during pregnancy leads to irreversible fetal neurologic effects and physical malformations in a cluster of symptoms called fetal alcohol syndrome. Fetal alcohol syndrome is a leading cause of intellectual disability in the United States and would explain this patient's behaviora l problems. Because of the failure of cell migration, fetal alcohol syndrome also presents with physica l abnormalities such as microcephaly, facial abnormalities (small palpebral fissures, thin vermi lion border, cleft lip and palate, smooth or long philtrum), limb deformities, and congenital heart disease. Patients with fetal alcoho l syndrome may demonstrate abnormal bone development (eg, cervical spine fusion) and delayed bone growth. Though alcohol is associated with obstetric complications such as preterm birth that commonly result from the use of substances during pregnancy, the physical malformations including those seen in this case are specific to alcohol use.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) (Choice A) is defined as a pattern of inattention or hyperactivity that persists in at least two settings. Patients may demonstrate symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty following instructions, difficulty completing tasks, or a poor attention span in school. Interrupting others, fidgeting, and not waiting one's turn may be symptoms of hyperactivity. This patient's behavioral problems are only seen at school and her unique physical characteristics are not seen in ADHD. Characteristic physical findings of Down syndrome (Choice B) include intellectua l disability, broad, flat, facial features with prominent epicanthal folds, and a single palmar crease. There are similarities between the abnormal facies of patients with fetal alcohol syndrome and Down syndrome, but this patient's combination of growth retardation and characteristic physica l features are most suggestive of fetal alcohol syndrome. - - - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 22-yea r-old college student comes to the physician because of depressed mood, restlessness, irritability, and an inability to concentrate since being raped 1 week ago. She has had difficulty sleeping because of recurrent nightmares about the rape and has not been able to study or attend classes . At times, she feels like the world around her is not real. Physical examination shows no abnormal ities. On mental status examination, she is anxious and tense. She is unable to remembe r the details of the rape and becomes distressed and does not want to talk about it. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Acute stress disorder refers to symptoms of intrusive thoughts or memories, changes in arousal and reactivity, avoidance of reminders of trauma, and negative changes in mood or thoughts that occur within 1 month of a traumatic event. The inciting traumatic event is defined as a serious physically or sexually violent experience. Intrusive memories may manifest as daytime flashbacks, nightmares, or dissociative experiences (eg, derealization as in this patient). Changes in arousal and reactivity may manifest as hypervigilance, easy startle, anxiety, restlessness, or decreased concentration. This patient's selective amnesia represents a negative alteration in cognition. Treatment common ly includes trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy rather than medication.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Brief psychotic disorder (Choice B) is characterized by at least one acute psychotic symptom (eg, delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior) lasting less than 1 month. This patient's belief that the world around her is not real is stress-related rather than rigid, signifying that the belief represents derealization rather than a delusion. Generalized anxiety disorder (Choice C) is an anxiety disorder that features excessive worrying about a range of topics with associated functional impairment. This patient's anxiety is specific to the rape. Major depressive disorder (Choice D) includes 2 or more weeks of five of the following symptoms: depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt or worthlessness, difficulty concentrating, psychomotor retardation, suicidal thoughts, or neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). This patient does not meet the symptom or duration criteria for major depressive disorder. Post-traumatic stress disorder (Choice E) refers to symptoms of intrusive thoughts and memories of trauma, hyperarousal, avoidance - - -- - - -- - - - - - - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - -- - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - - - r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 47-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of decreased libido over the past 2 years. He describes his marriage as good. He is able to achieve erection only through masturbation. He does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. He uses marijuana daily. His pulse is 72/min, respirations are 10/min, and blood pressure is 120/90 mm Hg. Physical examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. Serum studies show a thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 1 µU/ml, thyroxine (T 4) concentration of 7 µg/dl, and triiodothyronine (T 3) concentration of 125 ng/dl. Urine toxicology screening is positive for marijuana. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Cannabis use has been associated with erectile dysfunction. The pathogenesis is believed to involve both peripheral vascular endothelial dysfunction and dysregulated endocannabinoid signaling in the hypotha lamus. Testicular atrophy and decreased libido related to cannabis use have been found in animal studies, though human studies of the relationship of cannabis and libido have demonstrated mixed results. Erectile function may be sufficient to allow for nocturnal erections and erections from direct penile stimulation but insufficient to permit the level of rigidity required for penetration. Management of erectile dysfunction requires addressing the underlying cause. To assist in determining the underlying cause and potentia lly addressing the problem, patients with erectile dysfunction who use cannabis should be advised to discontinue cannabis use.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Individual psychotherapy (Choice B) and marital therapy (Choice C) assist in addressing psychogenic causes of erectile dysfunction, which typically present with intact nocturnal and masturbation-induced erections. Marital therapy is unlikely to be helpful given the good relationship between the patient and his partner. This patient should first attempt discontinuing cannabis; if discontinuing cannabis does not lead to improved sexual function, then individual psychotherapy should be considered to address potentia l performance anxiety or another psycho logical cause. Levothyroxine therapy (Choice D) treats sexual dysfunction secondary to hypothyroidism. This patient demonstrates normal thyroid function tests. Sildenafi l therapy (Choice E) promotes vasodilation in the arteries of the corpora cavernosa. In patients with erectile dysfunction secondary to psycho logical causes or substance use, these underlying problems should be addressed first. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: Immediately after undergo ing operative repair of a right knee dislocation, a 42-year-o ld woman has severe pain. She has a history of heroin addiction and has been receiving therapy through a comm unity-based methadone maintenance program . Her methadone maintenance dose has remained constant for 2 years. She has no other history of medical or psychiatric illness. On examinat ion, she rates her pain as a 10 on a 10-point scale, a level that is consistent with that reported by other patients who have undergone this operative procedure. Admin istration of which of the following is most appropriate at this time?

choices.A: A decreased methadone dose and additiona l analges ia on a set schedule
choices.B: A decreased methadone dose and patient-control led analgesia
choices.C: An increased methadone dose and additiona l analgesia on a set schedule
choices.D: The patient's usual methadone maintenance dose and patient-controlled analgesia
choices.E: The patient's usual methadone maintenance dose only

correctExplanation: Methadone is an opioid receptor agonist with a long half-life. While it can be used to treat acute pain, it is often used to treat patients with opioid use disorder. While methadone is common ly dosed once daily when used to treat opioid use disorder, it only provides analgesia for 6 to 8 hours. Therefore, it is not solely efficient for the management of postoperative pain. Current recommendations for acute pain management in patients on methadone maintenance therapy include continuing the baseline methadone dose and supplementing pain control with other non-opioid and opioid agents as needed. Pain control may be more difficult in patients on chronic methadone therapy, as they common ly have cross-to lerance to other opioids. Therefore, continuing this patient's baseline methadone dose and adding a regimen of patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) would be appropriate to allow for sufficient pain relief. As her acute pain declines, the PCA can be weaned.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. A decreased methadone dose and additiona l analgesia on a set schedule (Choice A) would not effectively treat this patient's pain. A decreased dose of methadone would likely exacerbate her pain, and a set schedule of pain medication would not be adequate or flexible enough to control her pain. A decreased methadone dose and patient-controlled analgesia (Choice B) may control this patient's pain but would likely cause her to use an increased amount of intravenous opioids as compared with a regimen with her baseline dose of methadone. An increased methadone dose and additional analgesia on a set schedule (Choice C) may control this patient's pain but would complicate weaning of her medication regimen back to her baseline methadone dose. Additional ly, this patient has been on a stable dose of methadone and adjusting her dose may interfere with her substance use disorder treatment. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because of a 3-month history of social withdrawa l and subtle but increasingly odd interpersonal interactions, such as blinking to avoid direct eye contact. He also has a 1-month history of intermittent daydreaming and episodes of talking to himself. His behavior was first noticed by his teacher and the school nurse, who notified his parents. The patient says that when in quiet locations, he hears vague, distorted sounds. He talks to himself to calm himself and to make the sounds disappear. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His maternal uncle has bipolar disorder, and two paternal uncles have schizophrenia. The patient does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, he is alert and fully oriented; he appears shy and has a flat affect. He says his mood is "okay." Further testing is most likely to show which of the following results in this patient?

choices.E: Hyperphospho rylation of the Tau protein

correctExplanation: According to the DSM-5, patients with schizophreniform disorder must demonstrate two of following: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, or disorganized behavior (known as positive symptoms), or negative symptoms (eg, flat affect, apathy, alogia). To meet diagnostic criteria, patients must demonstrate symptoms for greater than 1 month and less than 6 months. Two-thirds of patients with schizophreniform disorder ultimately develop schizophrenia. Cognitive impairment is commonly one of the early signs of schizophrenia. Schizophrenia has been postulated to result from excessive pruning of glutamatergic synapses in the cerebral cortex during development, explaining the negative and cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia. Patients commonly experience deficits across several cognitive domains including attention, working memory, verbal learning and memory, and executive function. However, basic cognitive functions such as orientation commonly remain intact. Antipsychotic medications address positive symptoms but do not significantly improve negative or cognitive symptoms. Cognitive training may assist with cognitive deficits.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Abnormal amyloid precursor protein (Choice A) and hyperphosphorylation of the Tau protein (Choice E) are pathologic findings in dementia, Alzheimer type, not schizophrenia. questionStem: A 42-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examinat ion for insurance purposes. When asked for an emergency contact, he gives the name of his mother but says that she lives in another state and that he has not seen her for 5 years. He lives by himself and says that he has no friends. He spends most of his free time alone in his apartment cutting out articles about animals from magazines and newspapers that he plans to use in the future. He has worked the graveyard shift of his company for 10 years with few absences. On two occasions, he was offered a day shift but refused. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. He is wearing mismatched socks, and his glasses are tied to a piece of twine he wears around his neck. Physical examinat ion shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, he is alert and oriented to person, place, and time. His thoughts are goal directed but difficult to understand because of his frequent use of idiosyncratic metaphors. He reports no auditory or visual hallucinations. He can recall three of three objects after 5 minutes and describes events of the past several years without difficulty. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Schizotypal personality disorder is a cluster A personality disorder, the odd or eccentric cluster. The disorder is characterized by odd behavior and thinking and a constricted affect. Patients with schizotypa l personality disorder may have strange, overly metaphorical or magical thinking, though they fluctuate in the degree of their conviction about these beliefs (which differentiates these beliefs from the fixed delusions of schizophrenia). The strange beliefs may also manifest as eccentric appearance as in this patient. Patients may experience somatosensory illusions or other abnormal perceptions. Patients with schizotypal personality disorder may appear to lack interest in cultivating relationships (eg, work graveyard shifts) and, because of an inability to interpret others' motivations, may be deeply distrustful and anxious around others. Personality disorders are persistently maladaptive ways of relating to the self and to society that typically appear by early adulthood.

questionStem: A 47-yea r-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of anxiety and difficulty falling asleep. He attributes his symptoms to the stress related to his 21-year-old daughter's weddi ng plans. He divorced his wife 11 years ago because he felt more sexually attracted to men than women. He has had a monogamous homosexua l relationsh ip for 7 years. He relates that he is happier now than when he was married, but he has been having some doubts recently. He would like to bring his partner to the weddi ng and accompa ny his daughter down the aisle, but the groom's parents are protesti ng his attendance. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Adjustment disorder refers to the onset of an emotional disturbance within 3 months of an identifiable stressor. The emotiona l disturbance manifests as marked distress out of proportion to the stressor and a significant impairment in daily school, work, or social functioning. Patients may internalize or externalize their distress, resulting in depression and anxiety symptoms or conduct disturbances, respectively. Patients with adjustment disorder do not meet criteria of anxiety, depressive, or conduct disorders. This patient is experiencing distress and anxiety symptoms related to the possibi lity of difficulties with his daughter 's fiance 's parents at his daughter 's wedding because of his sexual orientation. As adjustment disorder is typical ly self-limited, the treatment of adjustment disorder commonly includes brief supportive psychotherapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. This patient does not demonstrate evidence of exhibitionistic disorder. Gender dysphoria (Choice C) refers to a difference between an individua l's assigned gender and gender identity that causes clinically significant distress or functiona l impairment. Though this patient experiences sexual attraction to men, there is no evidence that he possesses a gender identity different from his assigned gender as a man. Generalized anxiety disorder (Choice D) is an anxiety disorder that features excessive worrying about a range of topics with associated functional impairment. This patient's anxiety is specific to his daughter's wedding. questionStem: A 67-year-o ld woman with major depressive disorder is brought to the physician by her daughter for a follow-up examination. During the past 6 months, she has received trials of citalopram, fluvoxam ine, and escitalopram with no improvement in her symptoms. Four weeks ago, she was switched from fluoxetine to sertraline therapy because the fluoxetine caused excessive tiredness . Her daughter reports that the patient is "slightly better, but not dramat ically so." She has had a decreased appetite resulting in a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss during the past 3 months. Today, her eyes are closed throughout most of the visit. She appears cachectic and disheve led. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 43 kg (95 lb); BMI is 16 kg/m2. Physical examinat ion shows poor skin turgor and severe psychomotor retardat ion. On menta l status exam ination, she respo nds to few of the physician's questions and uses only brief responses . There is no evidence of suicida l ideation or psychot ic symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Add buprop ion to her current medicat ion regimen
choices.B: Add olanzapine to her current medication regimen
choices.C: Switch from sertraline to nortripty line
choices.D: Switch from sertraline to paroxet ine

correctExplanation: Symptoms of major depressive disorder (MOD) include two or more weeks of at least five of the following symptoms: depressed mood, anhedonia (eg, decreased interest in socia lizing), guilt or worth lessness, difficu lty concentrating, suicidal thoughts, or neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). These symptoms disrupt everyday functioning. This patient's functional impairment is so severe that she is minimal ly interactive and appears disheveled. Her neurovegetative symptoms have led to physical deterioration, including significant weight loss and nutritiona l compromise. The patient requires admission to the psychiatric unit to prevent further physica l deterioration and so she can receive an inpatient course of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). ECT utilizes electrical current to induce a generalized seizure under general anesthesia, which is postulated to increase monoamine activity and promote neurogenesis. Indications include depression that is refractory to multiple medication classes and depression associated with catatonia, nutritional compromise and dehydration, psychotic features, or persistent suicida l intent. Depression may begin to improve immediately after the first ECT session, whereas antidepressant medication takes weeks to work. Further, ECT has an increased effectiveness compared with antidepressant medications. Adverse events common ly include transient memory loss and the risks of general anesthesia (eg, cardiovascu lar events, postoperative confusion).
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Adding bupropion or olanzapine to an antidepressant regimen (Choices A and B) are augmentation strategies utilized in patients with a significant partial response to the initial antidepressant. This patient minimal ly responded to sertraline. Further, these augmentation strategies typically take weeks to be effective, whereas this patient is nutritiona lly compromised and requires rapid treatment. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 52-year-o ld man with angina pectoris comes for a follow-up examination. His wife reports that he is concerned that his neighbors have been watching and videotaping him over the past 3 months. He has no history of these concerns prior to this time. He has suggested to his wife that they build a 14-foot fence to stop this surveillance, but she is not concerned that they are being videotaped. He believes that the neighbors might have followed him to his appointment today, but he does not believe that they would come into the office and speak to the office personnel. His medications include metoprolol and aspirin. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, he is guarded and hypervigilant. He is oriented to person, place, and time. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.C: Mood disorder due to a general medical condition

correctExplanation: Delusional disorder is characterized by the presence of one or more delusions (fixed, false beliefs) for a month or longer without other psychotic symptoms (eg, hallucinations). Patients typically lack significant negative symptoms (eg, alogia, apathy) or functional impairment. The onset of psychotic symptoms in patients older than 45 years is often consistent with delusional disorder (or a medical cause of psychosis) rather than schizophrenia. The disorder may present suddenly or gradually. Patients typically lack insight into their illness and may resist seeking psychiatric help, though antipsychotic medication and psychotherapy are the preferred treatments.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Brief psychotic disorder (Choice A) is characterized by at least one acute psychotic symptom (eg, delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior) lasting less than 1 month. Mood disorder due to a general medical condition (Choice C) refers to depression or mania secondary to a medical disease. This patient does not demonstrate symptoms of depression or mania, instead presenting with an isolated delusion. Schizotypal personality disorder (Choice D) is a cluster A personality disorder, the odd or eccentric cluster. The disorder is characterized by odd or magical behavior and thinking, along with a constricted affect. Rigid delusions are more consistent with delusional disorder. As well, patients with personality disorders demonstrate a persistent pattern of interpersonal difficulties that typically begins early in life.
